readings.sections_read: p1 introductory correction discussion; pp4–5 context/cost; p9 credibility intervals; p10 local validity advice
readings.confirmed: Structured interviews retain a high mean validity, but the reported .42 mean has an80% credibility interval .18–.66 across settings. This is heterogeneity, not a95% confidence interval on the mean. Authors also discuss development time, cost and applicant context.
readings.limits: No numerical transfer to software recommendations or LLM procedures; this reinspection does not count as another method paper.

readings.sections_read: abstract; results atp4; Table1 atp5; discussion p6
readings.confirmed: In the ECG verification comparison, both conditions had89 interpretations; net errors corrected were26 with checklist and3 without. Verification took63 versus35 seconds and added more characters.
readings.limits: Fifteen experts and repeated ECG interpretation; improved error correction does not mean shorter output or lower elapsed time. Not a human review measurement in AF-RES-018.

readings.sections_read: objective/methods pp0–1; results p5; COMMENT p6
readings.confirmed: The antiplatelet recommendation example lagged cumulative evidence by10 years and the first published meta-analysis by6 years. The discussion identifies evidence volume, publication lag and differing endpoints as possible explanations.
readings.limits: Retrospective cumulative reconstruction and expert reviews were not randomized or matched in information/search budget. Different endpoints can explain some disagreement.

readings.sections_read: Tables2–4, section3.1–3.3, PDF lines168–247
readings.confirmed: The paper distinguishes pairwise preference from individual scoring, and documents position/name bias on deliberately similar answers. Randomized labels alone are not a proof of invariant judgment.
readings.limits: These 2023 pairwise tests do not estimate bias in current individual software-candidate relevance labels.

readings.sections_read: Definition section2.1 and limitations5.2, PDF lines85–97 and490–521
readings.confirmed: Self-preference needs quality control; the authors distinguish capability-level causal evidence from the unproven claim that any particular example is preferred because it is recognized.
readings.limits: Summarization and fine-tuning experiments; same underlying generator for A/P means no automatic directional bias can be assumed.

readings.sections_read: Section3 experimental design and Table2, HTML lines121–156
readings.confirmed: Repeated trials, order changes and task/model variation distinguish stability from position consistency. Effects differ across judges and tasks.
readings.limits: The temperature and comparison settings differ from this workspace. One randomized order without reruns cannot identify a causal position effect here.

readings.sections_read: Section3 length-controlled estimator, HTML lines94–129
readings.confirmed: Length-controlled AlpacaEval estimates a regression-adjusted counterfactual with model, length and instruction terms. It is not produced by simply truncating text.
readings.limits: Our30-word normalization is a separate intervention and may remove qualifications; it does not inherit this estimator’s validation or remove all style bias.

readings.sections_read: Task C relevance definitions and annotation protocol, PDF lines326–426
readings.confirmed: The benchmark separates directly answering a subquestion from potentially useful context, employs at least three annotators and hidden checks, and reports an annotation-interface confusion between related and original questions.
readings.limits: Its Good/Bad merger is not our2/1/N/0 adoption codebook; human agreement there does not validate internal labels here.

readings.sections_read: Section3.1 and Table2, PDF lines143–209
readings.confirmed: The reference is the highest-voted eligible answer; additional valid-by-vote answers often exist. Retrieved supporting pages exclude Reddit itself.
readings.limits: Votes and reference selection do not establish actual adoption; this work is long-form explanatory QA rather than software deployment.

readings.sections_read: Sections1–3, PDF lines50–145
readings.confirmed: The methodological critique explains how system-order correlations and popularity-based pools can hide reversals for the strongest systems. Comparing similarity to an evaluator is not the same as validating user relevance.
readings.limits: This is an authored methodological argument and synthesis, not an institutional prohibition or a measured effect for the current model.

readings.sections_read: Introduction and Section2.1, PDF lines44–114
readings.confirmed: Incomplete relevance judgments and disappearance of documents are distinct problems. Fixed-depth precision has a different denominator and discrimination from recall-based measures.
readings.limits: The paper does not make a purposive software recommendation sample complete, nor justify replacing preregistered recall with a post hoc preferred metric.

readings.sections_read: Section5.2, PDF lines546–637 and627–693
readings.confirmed: The comparison requires a statistic matching the reported estimand; median and mean differences can yield different tests. The reported agreement between methods used50 topics, and the authors explicitly warn about smaller topic sets and bootstrap p-values.
readings.limits: Our registered percentile intervals are descriptive question-cluster uncertainty, not this paper’s p-value test or a proof of population equivalence.

readings.sections_read: Section3.1–3.2 and pilot experiment5.2.1–5.2.2, PDF lines201–299 and1077–1159
readings.confirmed: The paper separates power, effect size, topic count and judging effort; its pilot-based cost prediction sometimes underestimates and sometimes overestimates actual judgments.
readings.limits: Its hypothetical/adaptive resource allocation and TREC validation do not increase the independent question count in our fixed-purpose sample.

readings.sections_read: Sections4.6–5.3, PDF lines628–740
readings.confirmed: A positive LLM-judging case uses a locally configured model, calibrated prompts, external real-searcher preference pairs and ongoing audits. External searcher labels let the authors distinguish third-party disagreement from third-party error.
readings.limits: The operating costs and2.5million preference pairs cannot be transferred to53 software questions or interpreted as evidence of our labels’ correctness.

readings.sections_read: Results and Discussion, PDF lines161–210 and272–324
readings.confirmed: Reconsidering optimality using topic-set splits changes which test is safest, most powerful or closest to its nominal error criterion. The authors note that their global error measure approximates, rather than directly establishes, TypeI error.
readings.limits: No single test is certified best for all outcomes; choosing whichever analysis supports P would violate the frozen plan.

readings.sections_read: PDF lines60–124, objective exceptions and calibration
readings.confirmed: Broken-leg exceptions are possible when objective and correctly recognized; this argument does not justify arbitrary post-hoc clinical overrides.
readings.limits: Conceptual boundary argument, not a randomized test of this structured LLM procedure.

readings.sections_read: PDF lines331–413, shrinkage and criteria heterogeneity
readings.confirmed: Under stringent shrinkage to entirely new samples, the mechanical advantage was eliminated for two outcomes rather than reversed. Aggregated criteria differ.
readings.limits: Selection/admissions validity and combination formulas are not equal-budget search workflows.

readings.sections_read: PDF lines666–688, interview validity by outcome
readings.confirmed: The reported job-performance validities are .51 for structured and .38 for unstructured interviews; training-performance estimates are about .35 for both.
readings.limits: Later corrections revise these estimates; outcome-dependent results cannot be transferred as software recommendation effect sizes.

readings.sections_read: PDF lines1192–1242, exceptional clinical wins and moderator
readings.confirmed: Seven of eight clinical wins supplied extra information, but extra information was not a statistically significant moderator over all136 studies.
readings.limits: The exceptional-win description does not establish that information inequality caused all differences.

readings.sections_read: PDF lines149–431, design and results
readings.confirmed: Fifty analysts were randomized25/25;20/25 controls independently reformatted evidence and16 used matrices. ACH covered more evidence but did not improve accuracy in this experiment.
readings.limits: Control already used structure; cannot treat this as structure versus no structure, or count its companion analysis as another sample.

readings.sections_read: Full-text HTML lines30–53, outcome Table2 and Discussion
readings.confirmed: Ontario data included109341 procedures before and106370 after. Adjusted mortality .71% to .65% and complications3.86% to3.82% were not statistically significant improvements; implementation differed from initial studies.
readings.limits: Null significance is not equivalence. Table2 adjusted comparisons and additional regression estimates have different P values; OCR also misrenders one complication confidence bound.

readings.sections_read: PDF section5.7, Tables14–15, lines1261–1380
readings.confirmed: Sentence-level attribution took258.1 versus203.7 seconds. Fifty expert-labeled cases did not establish quality improvement; model order stayed the same.
readings.limits: This is an annotation-task comparison, not reader time for software recommendation lists.

readings.sections_read: v1 Methods3.2.3–3.2.5 and Discussion, lines92–112 and175–187
readings.confirmed: Statements were atomized and checked against every source in a response. The paper explicitly measures source support rather than direct factual correctness.
readings.limits: Use only v1; unsupported includes absent evidence and is not equivalent to false. Our current-official-document claim audit measures a different construct.

readings.sections_read: Methods pp1–2 and limitations pp7–8, lines87–114 and431–509
readings.confirmed: The comprehensive pathway checklist used6 intervention and5 control hospitals; implementation required6–9 months. The authors discuss local compliance, reporting differences, pre/post confounding and substantial organizational work.
readings.limits: Observed outcome improvement cannot be attributed to a form alone; no patient-randomized design and no direct transfer of effect size to LLM search.

readings.sections_read: Methods pp1–3; Results and Figure1 pp3–4; implementation discussion p6
readings.confirmed: Seventeen teams performed106 simulated crises. Critical steps omitted were24/371 with versus89/379 without checklists; analysis accounted for clustering and scenario differences.
readings.limits: Simulation outcome is process adherence, not clinical mortality. Local adaptation, training and interface were not incidental implementation details.

readings.sections_read: Metrics2.5 and Results3.1–3.2, PDF lines507–631
readings.confirmed: ACH did not significantly improve mean absolute probability error: reported difference .04 with95% interval−.02 to.11. Both groups showed incoherence, with point estimates favoring controls.
readings.limits: The benchmark assumes conditional independence for its Bayesian target. Same50 analysts asSTR03; do not count two independent experiments.

readings.sections_read: PDF Table2 and noise/decomposition discussion pp8–9, lines308–394
readings.confirmed: The authors argue that reducing one bias can activate its opposite and that subjective decomposition can carry noise into apparently structured matrices.
readings.limits: Conceptual analysis with cited examples, not a newly randomized equal-budget comparison or proof that decomposition always harms.
